headline: A war crimes judge wins the Nobel Peace Prize.
summary: Navi Pillay, a South African judge in her mid-80s, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. She sat on the International Criminal Court and the Rwanda tribunal. The committee said she has been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted." Trump, who wanted it, did not win.

cover_question.q: Why does a judge get a peace prize?

cover_answer: For making sure war crimes went to trial.
table_question: Does a rule count if the strongest player ignores it?

5-7.script: A judge from South Africa named Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize today. For years her job was to make sure that when people did terrible things in a war, they had to go to court for it, like a referee who writes the foul down so it counts. She is in her 80s and she is still at it. That is a good day.
5-7.why: A judge is a referee for grown-ups, and a prize for a fair one is a story a six-year-old can hold whole.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script turns her life's work into one picture: the referee who writes the foul down so it counts. "Court" and "fair" arrive attached to a person with a name and an age. Expect "what did the bad people do?" Hurt people in a war, and a judge dealt with it.

8-12.script: Navi Pillay was the first Black woman on South Africa's highest court. She judged war crimes at the Rwanda tribunal and the International Criminal Court. The Nobel committee says that got those crimes prosecuted. A referee for countries, and the prize says the calls stood.
8-12.why: A career as a chain of referees, each for a bigger game.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether rules apply to everyone, so the script runs her career as a chain: a national court, then a tribunal, then a court for all countries. The referee is the mechanism they know, and the prize is the crowd agreeing the calls were right. Expect "who makes countries obey?" Nobody, fully.

13-17.script: Can a court with no army keep the peace? Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize for making sure war crimes went to trial, at the International Criminal Court among others. Trump sanctioned that court and called it "rogue" and "evil". Second: is a prize you campaign for, as Trump did, still a prize?
13-17.why: Two arguments: law without force, and a prize you campaign for.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can reason about what is not in front of them, so the script asks whether a court with no army is still a court, Pillay's work on one side, Trump's sanctions on the other. The second question, a prize you campaign for, is small enough to argue at the table. Expect "did Trump deserve it?" Say what you think.

5-7.a: A prize given once a year to someone who helped the world toward peace. This year it went to a judge who made sure wrongs in a war went to court.

8-12.q: Why does a judge get a peace prize?
8-12.a: The committee says she made sure war crimes got prosecuted.

13-17.q: Why did Trump sanction the court she sat on?
13-17.a: Axios doesn't say. He called the ICC "rogue" and "evil" last month.

13-17.q: Can you give your Nobel to someone else?
13-17.a: No. Machado gave Trump her medal, but the prize itself can't move.
